query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy nanoalloys (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi base) doped with minor Al or Ti additions and heated to 700–1100 °C, local short-range clustering of the minor elements—combined with high configurational entropy—suppresses diffusion-driven grain coarsening and phase segregation, thereby enhancing structural and chemical stability at elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A near-equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy in nano-crystalline form with initial average grain size of ~10 nm, produced via mechanical alloying or co-sputtering methods.
generation.intervention: Systematically incorporate 0–5 at.% Al or Ti while ramping temperature from 700 °C up to 1100 °C in an inert atmosphere to assess the influence of minor-element doping.
generation.conditions: In-situ TEM combined with parallel MD simulations under inert atmosphere and controlled compositions, with real-time imaging at incremental temperature steps (700–1100 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: Minor-element-induced short-range ordering and local lattice distortions that reduce effective diffusion rates and stabilize grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Elevated configurational entropy and local chemical ordering together inhibit atomic mobility, thus delaying grain coarsening and chemical segregation at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline CoCrFeMnNi nanoalloy, the doped variants retain smaller grain sizes and more uniform composition after extended annealing at 700–1100 °C, as observed by in-situ TEM imaging and supported by MD simulations indicating slower coarsening kinetics.
generation.baseline: Undoped CoCrFeMnNi nanoalloy subjected to identical thermal treatments.
generation.boundary: Above ~1100 °C or for minor additions exceeding 5 at.%, this stabilizing effect may diminish due to enhanced diffusivity or the formation of undesirable phases.
generation.uncertainty: Whether these beneficial effects scale to industrial-grade alloys with more complex impurity profiles and larger sample volumes remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoalloys: one with 5 at.% Al or Ti, and another without (baseline). Subject both sets to identical thermal cycling (700–1100 °C) under inert atmosphere in an in-situ TEM, while parallel MD simulations track atomic diffusion and cluster formation with temperature.
measurements: Real-time electron diffraction for phase identification during heating and cooling.
High-resolution imaging (TEM) for grain size evolution and possible phase segregation.
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy for local composition mappings.
Comparison of simulation-predicted and observed microstructural changes.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped alloys exhibit equivalent grain growth, phase separation, or microstructural coarsening compared to the baseline, and no significant reduction in measured diffusion or segregation is observed, then the hypothesized short-range clustering mechanism leading to enhanced stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

chosen.technique: In-situ high-temperature TEM with parallel MD simulations
chosen.conditions: Energy-filtered imaging and compositional mapping at 800–1200 °C in inert atmosphere
chosen.why: A combined in-situ experimental and computational approach is most direct and standard in materials science for clarifying the mechanisms of structural and chemical stability. Real-time high-temperature TEM observations reveal morphological and chemical evolution, while parallel MD simulations provide atomistic insight. This synergy can test mechanistic hypotheses about how high configurational entropy, elemental interactions, and diffusion rates dictate nanoalloy stability at elevated temperatures.
